q: Where are the aircraft accident reporting rules actually written?
a: In 49 CFR Part 830, Notification and Reporting of Aircraft Accidents or Incidents and Overdue Aircraft, and Preservation of Aircraft Wreckage, Mail, Cargo, and Records. It is an NTSB rule in Title 49, not a Federal Aviation Regulation in Title 14. The AIM summarizes the same material under safety of flight, which is a fine place to look it up in the airplane, but the rule itself is 49 CFR Part 830.

q: Who writes Part 830 and who does it apply to?
a: The National Transportation Safety Board writes it, and it applies to the operator of any civil aircraft, and to certain public aircraft, within the United States and its territories. The duty to notify and to report falls on the operator, not on the FAA and not on the airport. On a rental or a flight you are conducting under Part 91, that is you as pilot in command and the owner between you; decide beforehand who makes the call.

q: Give me the Part 830 definition of an aircraft accident.
a: An occurrence associated with the operation of an aircraft that takes place between the time any person boards the aircraft with the intention of flight and the time all such persons have disembarked, in which any person suffers death or serious injury, or the aircraft receives substantial damage. Three triggers only: death, serious injury, substantial damage. 49 CFR 830.2, Definitions.

q: What is an incident, as Part 830 uses the word?
a: An occurrence other than an accident, associated with the operation of an aircraft, which affects or could affect the safety of operations. 49 CFR 830.2, Definitions. Every accident is also an occurrence affecting safety, but the word incident is reserved for the ones that fall short of death, serious injury or substantial damage. Only the listed incidents in 830.5 require immediate notification.

q: What is a fatal injury under Part 830, and why does the definition matter?
a: Any injury that results in death within 30 days of the accident, per 49 CFR 830.2, Definitions. It matters because an occurrence that was classified as an incident on the day it happened becomes an accident if an injured person dies inside that 30-day window, and the reporting obligation follows the reclassification.

q: List the serious injuries in 49 CFR 830.2.
a: Any injury that requires hospitalization for more than 48 hours beginning within 7 days of the injury; a fracture of any bone except simple fractures of fingers, toes or the nose; severe hemorrhage or nerve, muscle or tendon damage; injury to any internal organ; or second or third degree burns, or any burn affecting more than 5 percent of the body surface. Any one of the five makes the occurrence an accident.

q: A passenger breaks a finger getting out of the airplane after a hard landing. Accident?
a: No. A simple fracture of a finger, toe or nose is expressly carved out of the serious injury definition in 49 CFR 830.2, so that injury alone does not make it an accident. Check the other two triggers before you relax: if the hard landing also caused substantial damage, it is an accident on that ground, and if the person is hospitalized more than 48 hours it is an accident on that ground.

q: Define substantial damage.
a: Damage or failure that adversely affects the structural strength, performance or flight characteristics of the aircraft and would normally require major repair or replacement of the affected component. 49 CFR 830.2, Definitions. Note that it is a two-part test: the damage has to matter to the airplane's structure or how it flies, and it has to call for major repair or replacement.

q: What does Part 830 explicitly say is not substantial damage?
a: Engine failure or damage limited to an engine if only one engine is damaged; bent fairings or cowling; dented skin; small punctured holes in the skin or fabric; ground damage to rotor or propeller blades; and damage to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps, engine accessories, brakes or wingtips. 49 CFR 830.2, Definitions. That exclusion list is what makes most light airplane mishaps incidents rather than accidents.

q: You clip a runway light on landing. Is that reportable? Work it out for me.
a: Start with the accident definition in 49 CFR 830.2. Was anyone killed or seriously injured? No. Did the airplane receive substantial damage? A scuffed wheel pant, a nicked tire or a bent gear leg is on the express exclusion list, so it is not substantial damage. On those facts it is an incident, not an accident, and nothing in 830.5 requires immediate notification, so there is no NTSB report unless the Board asks for one.

q: Same runway light, but the strike buckles the firewall and wrinkles the skin behind it. Now?
a: Now it is an accident. Buckled structure affects the structural strength of the airframe and normally requires major repair or replacement, which is squarely the substantial damage definition in 49 CFR 830.2. That makes it an accident, which means immediate notification of the nearest NTSB office under 830.5, preservation of the wreckage under 830.10, and a written report within 10 days under 830.15.

q: The runway light you hit turns out to cost the airport $40,000 to repair. Does that change anything?
a: Yes. 49 CFR 830.5, Immediate notification, lists damage to property other than the aircraft estimated to exceed $25,000 for repair, or fair market value in the event of total loss, whichever is less. Above that figure you must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately even though the occurrence is only an incident, and you file a written report only if the Board requests one.

q: What is the honest short answer on whether hitting a runway light is reportable?
a: That it depends, and here is the test. It is reportable as an accident only if someone was killed or seriously injured or the airplane took substantial damage, and gear, wheels, tires, flaps and wingtips are excluded from substantial damage by name. It is reportable as a listed incident if the damage to the light and its cabling exceeds $25,000. Otherwise you tell the airport and the operator, and nobody files with the NTSB.

q: Run the 49 CFR 830.5 immediate notification list for me.
a: Any accident, plus these incidents: flight control system malfunction or failure; inability of any required flight crewmember to perform duties because of injury or illness; turbine engine failure releasing debris other than out the exhaust; in-flight fire; in-flight collision; property damage other than the aircraft over $25,000; release of a propeller blade other than by ground contact; loss of more than half the cockpit displays; and an overdue aircraft believed to have been in an accident.

q: Who exactly do you notify after an accident, and how fast?
a: The operator must notify the nearest NTSB field office immediately and by the most expeditious means available, per 49 CFR 830.5. In practice that is a phone call; the NTSB publishes a 24-hour number and field office list, and a call to ATC or to the FSDO does not discharge the obligation even though both will certainly find out. Have the number in your flight bag, not on a website you cannot reach from a field.

q: What information does the NTSB want in that first notification?
a: 49 CFR 830.6 lists it: aircraft type, nationality and registration marks; names of the owner and operator; name of the pilot in command; date and time; last point of departure and intended point of landing; position with reference to an easily defined geographic point; number aboard, number killed and number seriously injured; nature of the accident, the weather and the extent of damage so far as known; and a description of any explosives, radioactive materials or other dangerous articles carried.

q: When is a written report due, and on what form?
a: Within 10 days after an accident the operator files NTSB Form 6120.1 with the Board, per 49 CFR 830.15, Reports. If an aircraft was overdue and is still missing, the report goes in after 7 days. For an incident, even one that required immediate notification, a written report is filed only when an authorized representative of the Board requests one.

q: Does reporting to the NTSB take care of your obligation to the FAA?
a: No, they are separate. Part 830 is the NTSB's rule. Separately, 14 CFR 91.3, Responsibility and authority of the pilot in command, says that a pilot who deviates from a rule in an emergency must send a written report to the Administrator on request. The FAA may also open its own inquiry into airman and airworthiness issues, and a NASA ASRS report, filed within 10 days, is a separate voluntary action again.

q: What does Part 830 require you to do with the wreckage?
a: 49 CFR 830.10, Preservation of aircraft wreckage, mail, cargo and records, makes the operator responsible for preserving the wreckage, cargo, mail and all records until the NTSB takes custody. You may disturb it only to rescue people, to protect the wreckage from further damage, or to protect the public from injury, and if you do move anything you should make sketches, notes and photographs first.

q: You have just walked away from an off-airport landing. First actions?
a: People first, then the airplane, then the phone calls. Account for everyone and treat injuries; get clear of fuel; shut off the master, magnetos and fuel selector before you leave the cockpit; make sure the ELT is transmitting or switch it on manually; stay with the airplane, which is far easier to find than you are. Then notify the nearest NTSB office if 49 CFR 830.5 requires it, and tell the operator and your insurer.

q: The examiner asks where you would look up accident reporting in the airplane. What do you say?
a: That the rule is 49 CFR Part 830 and I carry it on my tablet, and that the AIM repeats the substance of it in the safety of flight chapter, which is where it turns up if you search the FAR/AIM app. I would name 49 CFR Part 830 first and the AIM second, because an examiner asking this question is usually checking that you know the reporting rule is not in Part 91 at all.

q: What are the two kinds of stress a pilot has to watch for?
a: Acute and chronic. Acute stress is the immediate, short-term response to a present demand, and it ends when the demand ends. Chronic stress is a continuing level of demand that the person cannot resolve, carried for weeks or months. Some texts split out a third, episodic or intermittent stress, for recurring bouts of acute stress. The PHAK's aeronautical decision making chapter covers both.

q: Give me a real example of acute stress in the cockpit.
a: An alternator light on a night cross country; a runway change on short final; a passenger getting sick; the gust that drops a wing in the flare. Each is a single, identifiable demand that arrives and then passes. In small doses acute stress sharpens you, raising heart rate and attention; in large doses it narrows attention to one thing and you stop flying the airplane while you solve the problem.

q: Give me a real example of chronic stress in a pilot's life.
a: A marriage coming apart, a job in doubt, money trouble, a sick parent, or a certificate program you are behind on and paying for. None of it is in the airplane and all of it comes with you. Chronic stress is corrosive because it has no end point, it degrades sleep, and the pilot stops noticing it, which is exactly why IMSAFE asks the question out loud instead of leaving it to feel.

q: How does acute stress change the way you fly?
a: It triggers the fight-or-flight response: heart rate and breathing rise, blood sugar rises, attention narrows. A moderate amount improves reaction time; past that the effects are attention tunneling, fixation on one instrument or one problem, and loss of the big picture. Classic symptoms are task saturation, missed radio calls, and reverting to the first action that comes to mind rather than the right one.

q: How does chronic stress change the way you fly?
a: It shows up as fatigue, poor sleep, irritability, slow decisions, and a flat, indifferent approach to risk, and it lowers the amount of acute stress you can absorb before you are overloaded. A pilot carrying chronic stress has used up most of his margin before he gets to the airport, so a routine diversion or a stuck alternator pushes him straight into saturation.

q: How do the two kinds of stress interact?
a: They stack. Chronic stress consumes the reserve you need for the acute events of a flight, so the same alternator failure that a rested pilot handles as a nuisance becomes an emergency for a pilot who has not slept properly in a month. The dangerous combination is chronic stress plus a new acute demand, which is the pattern behind a lot of loss of control accidents that read on paper as pilot error.

q: Where does stress sit in the IMSAFE check?
a: S is for stress, and the question is not whether you feel stressed but whether anything is occupying attention that belongs to the flight. Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue and emotion in the same checklist all feed stress, so a yes on any of them is usually a yes on S too. IMSAFE is a go/no-go check on the pilot and it has only one output: fly, or do not fly.

q: What do you actually do about stress before a flight?
a: Treat it as a hazard with mitigations rather than a mood. Remove sources you can remove, build margin into the flight, add fuel and time, brief yourself on the things most likely to go wrong, and set the no-go criteria before you are under pressure rather than during. If the stress is chronic, the honest mitigation is to stop flying for a period and deal with the cause; a commercial pilot who cannot say that out loud will eventually say it to an investigator.

q: Why is stress more dangerous to a commercial pilot than to a private pilot?
a: Because a commercial pilot is paid, and payment adds external pressure to every other source of stress: a customer waiting, a schedule, a reputation, an income. The stress and the external pressure feed each other, and the result is a pilot who launches into weather he would have declined as a private pilot. Naming the pay as a hazard on the PAVE checklist is the professional move.

q: How does stress relate to the hazardous attitudes?
a: Stress is the fuel; the hazardous attitudes are how it comes out. A stressed pilot reaches for impulsivity because deciding fast ends the discomfort, or resignation because nothing he does seems to matter. The antidotes still work but you have to remember them, which is harder under load, so the defense is to run the checklist rather than rely on judgment when you can feel yourself under pressure.

q: What is a KOEL?
a: The Kinds of Operation Equipment List. It is a table in the Limitations section, Section 2, of a GAMA-format pilot's operating handbook and FAA approved airplane flight manual, and it lists, by kind of operation, the equipment that must be installed and operable for that operation. Typical columns are VFR day, VFR night, IFR day, IFR night and sometimes flight into known icing, with the number of each item required.

q: Where exactly do you look for the KOEL, and what else lives near it?
a: Section 2, Limitations, of the AFM or POH, usually right after the weight, CG and maneuver limitations. Do not confuse it with the equipment list in Section 6, which is an inventory of everything installed in that individual airplane with weights and arms, nor with the airworthiness limitations in Section 4 of the maintenance manual. The KOEL says what is required; the equipment list says what is fitted.

q: Does every airplane have a KOEL?
a: No, and that is the point of the question. The kinds of operation equipment list arrived with the GAMA standardized handbook format in the late 1970s, so many older certificated airplanes have an airplane flight manual with no Section 2 table at all, and some handbooks print only a short kinds of operation paragraph instead. Open the book before you assert that the airplane has one.

q: If the airplane has no KOEL, what governs required equipment?
a: You fall back to the regulation and the paperwork. 14 CFR 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements, is the floor; then whatever the type certificate data sheet and the airplane's own equipment list require; then anything made mandatory by an airworthiness directive or required by the supplement to a supplemental type certificate; then any rule tied to the specific operation, such as 91.215 for a transponder.

q: Does any regulation actually mention the KOEL by name?
a: Yes. 14 CFR 91.213, Inoperative instruments and equipment, at paragraph (d)(2), requires that the inoperative item not be indicated as required on the aircraft's equipment list or on the Kinds of Operations Equipment List for the kind of operation being conducted. That is why the KOEL is not optional trivia: it is one of the four tests you have to pass before you fly with something inoperative and no minimum equipment list.

q: An item is on the KOEL for VFR night but you are flying VFR day. Does it have to work?
a: Not on that account. The list is organized by kind of operation, so only the column for the operation you are conducting applies. If the item is required only for VFR night and you fly day VFR, the KOEL does not require it, and you then go on to check 91.205 for day VFR, the equipment list, any applicable airworthiness directive, and finally 91.213(d) to placard and deactivate it properly.

q: Does your handbook have a kinds of operation list, and what does it say?
a: Yes. Section 2.19 says the airplane may be operated day or night VFR and day or night IFR when the appropriate equipment is installed and operable, and then lists the equipment by kind of operation: twelve items for day VFR, with position, instrument and anti-collision lights added for night VFR, a vacuum pump and gyro suction indicator added for day IFR, and both sets combined for night IFR.
dup: What kinds of operation is this airplane approved for?

q: Read me the day VFR equipment list out of your handbook.
a: Airspeed indicator; altimeter; magnetic compass; tachometer; oil pressure indicator; oil temperature indicator; fuel pressure indicator; fuel quantity indicator for each tank; volt-ammeter; elevator and rudder trim indicator; alternator; and a safety restraint for each occupant. Twelve items, and note that fuel pressure and the volt-ammeter are on this list even though 91.205 does not ask for them.

q: If the handbook lists the equipment, why does 91.205 still apply?
a: Because the handbook list is the type certification basis and the regulation is the operating rule, and you must satisfy both. The handbook says so itself: the note under Section 2.19 states that the list does not include the flight instruments and communication and navigation equipment required by the Part 91 and Part 135 operating rules. So an ELT, a transponder where required and shoulder harnesses come from the regulation, not from the handbook.
dup: If the handbook lists required equipment, why does 91.205 still matter?

q: Is a flap position indicator required on this airplane?
a: No. Walk it through: there is no minimum equipment list, so start with 14 CFR 91.205(b) for day VFR and run the mnemonic; 91.205 requires a landing gear position indicator on a retractable, and says nothing at all about flaps. Then check the handbook's kinds of operation list, which does not list one, then the equipment list and any airworthiness directive. Nothing requires it, so the airplane is legal without it.

q: Walk the 91.205 day VFR list and show me where a flap indicator would appear if it were required.
a: Airspeed indicator, tachometer, oil pressure gauge, manifold pressure gauge for an altitude engine, altimeter, temperature gauge for each liquid-cooled engine, oil temperature gauge for each air-cooled engine, fuel gauge for each tank, landing gear position indicator if the gear is retractable, anticollision lights, magnetic direction indicator, ELT, and safety belts and shoulder harnesses. Gear position is in there. Flap position is not.

q: Give me the general method for answering 'is this piece of equipment required?'
a: Five places, in order. 14 CFR 91.205 and any other operating rule that applies to the flight, such as 91.207 for the ELT or 91.215 for a transponder; then the kinds of operation equipment list in Section 2 of the handbook; then the airplane's own equipment list in Section 6; then any airworthiness directive or the flight manual supplement to an installed STC; and then, if it is inoperative, 91.213.

q: What is the title of 91.205 and what does it actually cover?
a: 14 CFR 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements. It applies to airplanes with a standard airworthiness certificate, which is why the rule does not govern an experimental or a limited category airplane in the same way. Paragraph (b) is VFR day, (c) adds VFR night, (d) adds IFR, and (e) covers flight at and above FL240.

q: An item is inoperative and the airplane has no MEL. What does 91.213(d) require?
a: Four tests. The item must not be part of the VFR-day type certification requirements; must not be listed as required on the equipment list or the kinds of operation equipment list for this operation; must not be required by 91.205 or any other rule for this flight; and must not be required to be operative by an airworthiness directive. Then it is removed or deactivated and placarded inoperative, and a pilot or mechanic determines it is not a hazard.
dup: You find an item inoperative and the aircraft has no minimum equipment list. What does 91.213 require?

q: Who may remove or deactivate the inoperative item, and who placards it?
a: Deactivation or removal is maintenance: it is done by a certificated mechanic or repair station unless it happens to be preventive maintenance a pilot may do under 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A. The placard reading INOPERATIVE goes on in either case, and the determination that the airplane is still safe for the flight is made by the pilot in command or by a mechanic. 14 CFR 91.213, Inoperative instruments and equipment.

q: Suppose the airplane did have a flap position indicator and it failed. May you fly?
a: Probably yes, but you have to run 91.213(d) rather than assume it. Check the VFR-day type certification requirements, the kinds of operation list, the equipment list and any AD. If it clears all four, deactivate or remove it, placard it INOPERATIVE and make the hazard determination, and then satisfy yourself operationally: without the indicator you confirm flap position by the handle detent, by the control feel, and by looking at the wing.

q: Why is 'the KOEL does not list it' not a complete answer on its own?
a: Because the KOEL is only one of the four tests in 91.213(d), and because some airplanes have no KOEL at all. An item can be absent from the KOEL and still be required by 91.205, by an airworthiness directive or by an STC supplement. The complete answer names the regulation first, then the handbook, then the equipment list, then the AD and STC paperwork, and says which one actually decided the question.

q: How do you know what the flaps are doing in this airplane without an indicator?
a: By the handle and by the airplane. The flaps are manually controlled by a handle between the front seats that locks into detents at 10, 25 and 40 degrees, so the number of notches you have pulled is the flap setting; the pitch change and the speed decay confirm it; and on a low wing you can see the flap itself from the cockpit. There is no electric motor and no position light to fail.

q: Does the manual flap system change your answer on required equipment?
a: It changes the practical answer, not the legal one. Legally you still work 91.205, the kinds of operation list, the equipment list and any AD. Practically, a cable-operated flap handle with mechanical detents is its own position indicator, which is why Piper never fitted one, and it is also why the flaps keep working after an alternator failure when the electric fuel pump, the stall warning horn and the radios are gone.

q: An examiner points at a piece of avionics and asks whether it is required. How do you structure the answer?
a: Name the sources in order rather than guessing. For this flight: 91.205 for day VFR, 91.207 for the ELT, 91.215 for the transponder, 91.225 and 91.227 for ADS-B Out where it is required, then the handbook's kinds of operation list, the equipment list, and any AD or STC supplement. If it is on none of those, it is not required, and if it is inoperative I still owe 91.213(d) a placard.

q: Is a second navigation radio required for your VFR cross country?
a: No. 14 CFR 91.205(b) requires no navigation radio at all for day VFR, and 91.205(c) adds nothing of the kind for night. Radios become required by the airspace and the kind of operation rather than by the equipment rule: two-way radio for Class B, C and D, a transponder with altitude reporting where 91.215 says so, and ADS-B Out where 91.225 says so. For VFR pilotage, a second radio is good practice, not a requirement.

q: What is a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit?
a: An operator permit for the person using an aircraft radio station, issued by the Federal Communications Commission, not the FAA, under 47 CFR Part 87, Aviation Services. It is a lifetime permit, it is held by the pilot rather than by the airplane, and it has nothing to do with your pilot certificate or medical. It is form FCC 605 and it is granted without a test.

q: When do you actually need a Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit?
a: For international operations. A pilot flying outside the United States, or operating an aircraft radio station on an international flight, needs the permit, and that is why it is on the list for a trip to the Bahamas, Canada or Mexico. It is not required for domestic flight within the United States, so it does not belong on the list of what you must have on your person to fly locally.

q: The examiner asks what you must have on your person to fly. Should you say radiotelephone permit?
a: No, and listing it is the classic giveaway. 14 CFR 61.3 requires a pilot certificate, an appropriate medical certificate or BasicMed documentation, and a government-issued photo identification, and that is the answer. Add the radiotelephone permit only if the examiner asks about international flight, and then say plainly that it is an FCC document required for operations outside the United States.
dup: What three documents must you have on your person to act as pilot in command?

q: Who issues the permit, how long is it good for, and what does it cost you to keep?
a: The FCC issues it under 47 CFR Part 87, Aviation Services. It is valid for the lifetime of the holder and there is nothing to renew, no examination and no recurrent requirement. Because there is no expiry and no test, a pilot who does any international flying should simply get one and put it in the flight bag rather than try to time it against a trip.

q: What is the difference between the operator permit and the aircraft radio station license?
a: The permit belongs to the person operating the radio; the station license belongs to the aircraft and is also issued by the FCC. On an international flight you need both: the airplane must hold a current aircraft radio station license and the pilot must hold the restricted operator permit. Domestically, neither is required of a U.S.-registered aircraft operating within the United States.

q: Is an FCC aircraft radio station license required for your Warrior?
a: Not for domestic flight. Since 1996 a U.S.-registered aircraft operating within the United States has not needed an FCC station license. It is required again as soon as the airplane leaves the country, so the Bahamas trip needs the station license in the airplane and the restricted radiotelephone operator permit in the pilot's pocket. 47 CFR Part 87, Aviation Services, is the FCC rule.
dup: When is an FCC radio station license required?

q: Which of the documents in ARROW is an FCC document?
a: None of them, and that is the trap. ARROW is the airworthiness certificate, registration certificate, radio station license if required, operating limitations and weight and balance data, and the R is the one that sometimes stands for the FCC station license, required only for international operations. The airworthiness and registration certificates are FAA documents; the operating limitations and weight and balance come from the manufacturer and the last weighing.

q: Define operational control.
a: 14 CFR 1.1, General definitions: operational control, with respect to a flight, means the exercise of authority over initiating, conducting or terminating a flight. It is not the same as holding the controls. The person with operational control decides whether the flight goes, where it goes, when it stops, and who flies it, and he carries the regulatory responsibility that goes with those decisions.
dup: What is operational control?

q: How do you tell who has operational control in a real arrangement?
a: Look at the decisions and the money, not the labels. Who decides whether the flight launches and whether to divert or cancel? Who selects, hires and pays the crew? Who holds the aircraft's maintenance responsibility and the insurance? Who bears the financial risk and takes the profit? The party that initiates, conducts and terminates the flight has operational control, whatever the contract calls itself.

q: Why is operational control the hinge question in any lease or rental scenario?
a: Because it decides which operating rule applies. If the customer has operational control and you are merely a hired pilot, the flight is Part 91 and your commercial certificate is enough. If you have operational control and you are also furnishing the aircraft for compensation, you are holding yourself out as an air carrier and the flight needs a certificate under Part 119 and operations under Part 135.

q: A customer who is not a pilot hires you to fly his own airplane. Legal on a commercial certificate?
a: Yes. You are providing pilot services only; the customer provides the aircraft and keeps operational control, so it is a Part 91 flight and 14 CFR 61.133, Commercial pilot privileges and limitations, lets you be paid for it. Confirm the practical items: that you are named on his insurance, that you meet the policy's open pilot requirements, that you are current and qualified in type, and that the airplane is airworthy.

q: You arrive and the owner's airplane is leaking oil and is not airworthy. He offers to rent one instead. May you fly it?
a: Maybe, and the question to ask is who will have operational control of the rented airplane. If the customer rents it in his own name, satisfies the FBO's requirements and still decides the flight, you remain a hired pilot on a Part 91 flight. If you rent it and then carry him for compensation, you are supplying both the aircraft and the crew for hire, which is carriage for hire and needs a Part 119 certificate.

q: Why can't the customer simply rent the airplane and hand you the keys?
a: Because the rental agreement usually will not let him. Most FBOs will only rent to a pilot who has been checked out and is named on the policy, and your customer is not a pilot. If the FBO rents to him anyway, read the agreement: if it requires that the FBO approve the pilot, or if the FBO is really furnishing aircraft and crew together, the FBO may be the one holding operational control, and now it is their certificate problem.

q: What is a dry lease?
a: A lease of the aircraft alone, with no crew. The lessee takes possession of the airplane and holds operational control, provides or hires the pilots himself, and operates under Part 91 if the operation otherwise qualifies. A genuine dry lease is the normal, legal way for a non-pilot owner or a company to put an airplane and a hired pilot together without needing an air carrier certificate.

q: What is a wet lease?
a: 14 CFR 110.2, Definitions, defines a wet lease as any leasing arrangement whereby a person agrees to provide an entire aircraft and at least one crewmember. Providing aircraft and crew together for compensation is carriage for hire, so a wet lease by someone without a Part 119 certificate is an illegal charter no matter what the paperwork calls it. The common dodge is a dry lease on paper with the lessor quietly supplying the pilot.

q: What makes a 'dry lease' a sham in the FAA's eyes?
a: When the paperwork says dry but the lessor keeps control of who flies, when it flies and whether it goes. Warning signs: the lessor supplies or approves the pilot, the lessor schedules and dispatches, the lessee pays a per-hour price that looks like a charter rate, the lessee never sees the maintenance decisions, and the lessee could not operate the airplane without the lessor's organization. The FAA looks at substance, not titles.

q: Does a truth-in-leasing clause apply to a Warrior lease?
a: No. 14 CFR 91.23, Truth-in-leasing clause requirement in leases and conditional sales contracts, applies to large civil aircraft, meaning more than 12,500 pounds maximum certificated takeoff weight. Your airplane is far below that. It is still worth knowing, because 91.23 is the rule that forces a lease to state who is responsible for operational control and for compliance, which is exactly the question you have to answer anyway.

q: The scenario keeps getting more complicated. What is the right professional answer?
a: To say out loud that the arrangement has become complex enough that I am not certain which rule applies, and then to decline the flight or get official guidance from the FSDO before flying it. An inspector will answer a question like this in writing. Guessing costs you a certificate; asking costs you a phone call, and a customer who will not wait for the answer is telling you something about the trip.

q: Why is 'I am only the pilot' not a defense if the operation turns out to be an illegal charter?
a: Because 14 CFR 91.3, Responsibility and authority of the pilot in command, makes you directly responsible for, and the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft, and enforcement actions in illegal charter cases routinely reach the pilot as well as the operator. You are the one who must determine which part you are operating under before you launch; nobody else on the ramp is going to do it for you.

q: What questions do you ask the customer before you accept a job like this?
a: Who owns or is renting the airplane and in whose name; who is paying for the airplane and who is paying me; who decides whether the flight goes and where; who is responsible for maintenance and for the airworthiness determination; am I named on the insurance and what are the open pilot requirements; and is there a written agreement I can read. If any answer is vague, the answer to the flight is not yet.

q: Which advisory circular would you point the customer at?
a: AC 120-12A, Private Carriage Versus Common Carriage of Persons or Property, which is where the four elements of common carriage and the meaning of holding out come from. For leasing specifically, AC 91-37, Truth in Leasing, explains what the parties to a lease have to get right about operational control. Neither is a regulation, but both are how the FAA says it will read the arrangement.
dup: Which advisory circular explains common carriage versus private carriage?

q: You see a stadium symbol on the sectional. What does it mean to you?
a: That there is a large stadium there, charted as a visual landmark, and that it carries a standing flight restriction whenever a qualifying sporting event is in progress. The chart does not draw the restricted airspace, because the restriction only exists while the event is on, so the symbol is a prompt to check NOTAMs for the day rather than an airspace boundary.

q: State the standing sporting event flight restriction.
a: No aircraft below 3,000 feet AGL within a 3 nautical mile radius of any stadium with a seating capacity of 30,000 or more people during a qualifying event, effective from one hour before the scheduled event time until one hour after the end of the event. It is published as a standing FDC NOTAM rather than being charted, and it is reissued and renumbered periodically.

q: Which events trigger the stadium restriction?
a: Major League Baseball, National Football League and NCAA Division One football games, and major motor speedway events such as NASCAR Sprint, Indy Car and Champ series races, at stadiums or speedways seating 30,000 or more. A high school game, a minor league game, a concert or a Division Two football game does not trigger it, though a separate TFR can always be issued for any of them.

q: What is the regulatory basis for the stadium restriction and for sporting event TFRs generally?
a: The standing stadium NOTAM is issued as a special security instruction under 14 CFR 99.7, Special security instructions. Separately, 14 CFR 91.145, Management of aircraft operations in the vicinity of aerial demonstrations and major sporting events, is the rule the FAA uses to put temporary restrictions around air shows and major sporting events by NOTAM. Cite both and say which one the stadium NOTAM uses.

q: Who may operate inside a stadium restriction?
a: Only the operations the NOTAM allows. Typically that is law enforcement and military aircraft supporting the event, air ambulance flights, aircraft operating under an ATC clearance for arrival or departure at an airport inside the restricted area, and approved event-related operations such as a broadcast or banner operator with a waiver. A transient VFR airplane without a reason to be there has none.

q: You are a commercial pilot and someone offers you money to tow a banner over a game. What is your answer?
a: That the stadium restriction forbids it unless the operation is specifically approved, so I would need the event's approval and an FAA waiver before I accepted the job. Banner towing is otherwise an operation a commercial pilot can be paid for without a Part 119 certificate, under the exception in 14 CFR 119.1(e), but the airspace restriction is a separate problem and the money does not solve it.

q: How do you find out whether a stadium restriction is active on your route today?
a: Check NOTAMs in the preflight briefing and look at the graphical TFR depiction, and read the FDC NOTAMs, not just the local field ones. The stadium restriction is time-based and tied to the event schedule, so you have to know when the game is. On a route that passes a charted stadium, the safe planning move is to route around it or above 3,000 feet AGL and not depend on the timing being what you expected.

q: What happens if you blunder through an active stadium restriction?
a: You may be intercepted, and you can expect a certificate action: a special security instruction issued under 14 CFR 99.7 has the force of a regulation, and 14 CFR 91.103, Preflight action, required you to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight. The defense that you did not know is the admission that you did not check NOTAMs. Squawk, listen on 121.5 and comply if you are intercepted.

q: Gusty wind splits two runways evenly. How do you choose the departure runway?
a: Compare them on headwind, crosswind and gust, then on what is off the departure end. Take the runway with a headwind component rather than any tailwind, and if the headwinds are equal, look at crosswind magnitude including gusts, runway length and surface, obstacles and terrain, the traffic flow in use, and where you would go if the engine quit. Then decide whether the result is inside your personal limits, not just the airplane's.

q: The wind is exactly between the two runways. What is left to decide it?
a: Everything that is not the wind. Runway length and width, slope and surface, the obstacle picture off each end, where the emergency landing options are, which runway the traffic is using, how long the taxi is with the wind on the tail, and which side the crosswind will be on. When the wind gives you no answer, the engine failure after takeoff should give you one.

q: On takeoff, does a crosswind from the left or from the right ask more of your right rudder?
a: From the left. The fin is behind the main gear and the center of gravity, so the airplane weathervanes into the wind: a left crosswind swings the nose left, and you hold the centerline with right rudder on top of the right rudder the left-turning tendencies already need. A right crosswind swings the nose right, which partly offsets P-factor, torque and slipstream. Say it that way and reason out loud; the examiner is watching the reasoning.

q: The prior candidate chose the runway with the wind from the left to save right rudder. Critique that.
a: The conclusion is defensible on other grounds but that reason is backwards. Weathervaning turns the nose into the wind, so a left crosswind increases the right rudder you need, it does not reduce it. What a left crosswind does give you is left aileron into the wind, whose down-going right aileron adds a little right-yawing drag, and that is a small effect. Choose the runway on components, length and emergency options, and get the rudder argument the right way round.

q: What do you do with the controls on a crosswind takeoff roll?
a: Full aileron into the wind as you start the roll, reducing it as the ailerons become effective, and rudder as needed to hold the centerline. Keep straight and keep the upwind wing down. Accelerate slightly past the normal rotation speed and lift off positively so the airplane does not settle back on one wheel, then establish a crab on the climbout. In this airplane the demonstrated crosswind is 17 knots.

q: Why does the emergency return matter when you pick the departure runway?
a: Because the wind that is a 15-knot crosswind on takeoff is the same 15-knot crosswind if you have to come back, and you will be coming back with a problem, probably low, possibly with partial power, on whichever runway you can reach. If the crosswind is marginal for a planned landing it is unacceptable for an unplanned one. Also look at what is straight ahead off each end: fields, water, trees, a city.

q: Is the maximum demonstrated crosswind component a limitation?
a: No. It is the strongest 90-degree crosswind in which the airplane was actually flown and shown to be controllable during certification, not a structural or regulatory limit, and on this airplane it is 17 knots from Section 4.5 and the cockpit placard. You may legally exceed it. Whether you should is a question about you, your currency and the day, and a school or an insurer may make it a hard limit anyway.
dup: What is maximum demonstrated crosswind component, and is it a limitation?

q: How do you compute crosswind and headwind components from the wind and the runway?
a: Find the angle between the wind direction and the runway heading, then crosswind equals wind speed times the sine of the angle and headwind equals wind speed times the cosine. Thirty degrees gives half the wind as crosswind, forty-five gives about 70 percent, sixty gives about 90 percent, and beyond sixty treat it as nearly all crosswind. The POH chart does the same thing graphically.

q: Wind 095 at 22 knots, runways 05 and 14. Work both.
a: Runway 05 is 050 magnetic, so the wind is 45 degrees off to the right; runway 14 is 140, so the wind is 45 degrees off to the left. Sine and cosine of 45 are both 0.707, so each runway sees a 15.6-knot crosswind and a 15.6-knot headwind. The wind genuinely splits them, so the decision has to come from the gust, the runway lengths, the obstacles and the side you want the crosswind on.

q: Wind 095 at 22 gusting 30, runway 05. Does the gust change your decision?
a: Yes, and it is the number that decides the flight. At 30 knots the crosswind component becomes 30 times 0.707, which is 21.2 knots, well above this airplane's 17-knot demonstrated crosswind. The gust, not the steady wind, is what you will be flying in the flare. I would say no to a departure that commits me to that crosswind on the return, and wait for it to come down or move the flight.

q: Wind 200 at 16, runway 05. What are the components?
a: Runway 05 is 050 and the wind is from 200, so the angle is 150 degrees, which means the wind is largely behind you. Crosswind is 16 times the sine of 150, which is 16 times 0.5, or 8 knots of crosswind and 13.9 knots of tailwind. A 14-knot tailwind is a long way outside what a Warrior's takeoff chart covers, so that runway is out; take the reciprocal.

q: Wind 040 at 20 on runway 36. Work it, and tell me what it means.
a: Forty degrees off the nose to the right. Crosswind is 20 times the sine of 40, which is 20 times 0.643, or 12.9 knots; headwind is 20 times the cosine of 40, which is 20 times 0.766, or 15.3 knots. So about 13 knots of crosswind and 15 knots of headwind. The crosswind is inside the 17-knot demonstrated figure, the headwind shortens the takeoff roll, and that runway is a reasonable choice.

q: How much does a tailwind hurt, and what does the handbook assume?
a: A great deal, and it is not symmetric with a headwind. The general planning rule is that a 10 percent tailwind component relative to liftoff speed increases the takeoff distance by roughly 20 percent, and landing distance grows the same way. The handbook's takeoff and landing charts are built for headwind components and usually only cover a small tailwind if any, so beyond that you are extrapolating, which you should not do.

q: The crosswind works out near 15 knots, gusting over 20. Would you be comfortable departing?
a: I would compute the components first and say the number out loud. With a steady crosswind near 15 knots and gusts putting it above the airplane's 17-knot demonstrated figure, my answer is no, for three reasons: the gust spread, not the steady wind, is what I have to fly; the same crosswind is waiting for me if I have to come straight back; and I have not flown a crosswind that strong recently enough to call myself proficient in it.

q: How do you read a time, fuel and distance to climb chart?
a: It is not a single lookup. The chart gives the time, fuel and distance accumulated in a climb from sea level at standard conditions up to the altitude you enter with, so you read it twice: once at the departure airport's pressure altitude and temperature, once at your cruise altitude and the temperature up there, and subtract the first set of numbers from the second. The difference is what the climb costs you.

q: Work an example of a climb computation for me.
a: Say the chart gives 4 minutes, 1.0 gallon and 6 nautical miles at the departure field's conditions, and 15 minutes, 3.2 gallons and 24 nautical miles at cruise altitude. Subtract: 11 minutes, 2.2 gallons and 18 nautical miles for the climb segment. Then add the handbook's allowance for start, taxi and run-up, which on this airframe is the 7-pound fuel allowance, a little over a gallon, on top of that.

q: Why do you have to subtract rather than just read the cruise altitude line?
a: Because the chart is cumulative from sea level and standard temperature, not from your airport. If you depart from a field at 3,000 feet and read only the 8,000-foot line, you have charged yourself for 3,000 feet of climb you never flew, which overstates time, fuel and distance. On a short leg out of a high airport that error is large enough to change the altitude you pick.

q: What does temperature do to the climb numbers?
a: Hot air raises density altitude, which costs you both lift and power, so the rate of climb falls and time, fuel and distance to climb all increase. Most charts give a correction, typically a percentage increase in time, fuel and distance for each given number of degrees above standard; some are plotted with temperature lines you enter directly. If the chart has no correction for your temperature you must not extrapolate past it.

q: What does altitude itself do to the climb?
a: Rate of climb decreases steadily with altitude as the normally aspirated engine loses power and the wing needs a higher true airspeed for the same indicated airspeed, so each successive thousand feet takes longer, burns more and covers more ground. Vx and Vy converge as you climb, and they meet at the absolute ceiling where rate of climb is zero. The service ceiling is where the best rate has fallen to 100 feet per minute.

q: What are the chart's assumptions, and what do you do about them?
a: A climb at the published climb speed, full throttle, mixture leaned per the handbook, a clean airplane, no wind, a level hard surface runway and a new airplane flown by a test pilot. Your airplane is 40 years old, you are not a test pilot, and the chart distance is still air distance. Add a margin, correct the distance for wind using groundspeed, and treat the result as a plan, not a promise.

q: The climb chart says 18 nautical miles in 11 minutes. There is a 20-knot headwind. Now what?
a: That 18 miles is a still air distance. Work it in groundspeed instead: at a climb speed of, say, 85 knots true with a 20-knot headwind, groundspeed is 65 knots, so 11 minutes covers 65 times 11 over 60, which is 11.9 nautical miles. The fuel and time do not change, but you are 6 miles short of where the chart put you, which matters when the first checkpoint is inside the climb.

q: How does the climb segment fit into your navigation log?
a: As its own leg. The climb has a different true airspeed, a different wind and a different fuel flow from cruise, so compute time, fuel and distance to climb from the chart, plot where top of climb falls along the first leg, and start the cruise calculation from there. If the whole first leg is inside the climb you never reach the cruise numbers at all, which is a common planning error on a short first leg.

q: Do you work time, fuel and distance to climb at the destination too?
a: Yes, if you are planning a climb there, and the examiner is likely to ask for both ends. At the destination you work the same chart with that field's pressure altitude and temperature to find what a go-around, a missed approach or a departure on the return leg would cost, and you work the takeoff and landing distances against the runway you will actually use there, in the conditions forecast for your arrival.

q: Your loading is legal on weight but the CG is close to the forward limit. What are your options?
a: Move weight aft or add weight aft. In order of preference: put the baggage in the baggage compartment instead of the back seat; move a passenger from the front to the rear seats; add ballast in the baggage compartment; or reduce weight that is forward of the CG. On this airplane the baggage compartment arm is 142.8 inches, far aft of everything else you can load, so it is the strongest lever you have.

q: Why is the baggage compartment such a powerful lever on this airplane?
a: Because of how far aft it is. The loading arms are 80.5 inches for the front seats, 118.1 for the rear seats, 95.0 for fuel and 142.8 for baggage, and the aft CG limit is 93.0 inches. Baggage sits almost 50 inches behind the aft limit, so every pound you put there moves the CG aft several times as effectively as the same pound in the back seat.

q: Work it: 1,900 pounds, CG at 83.2 inches, you add a 25-pound bag in the baggage compartment.
a: Old moment is 1,900 times 83.2, which is 158,080 inch-pounds. The bag adds 25 times 142.8, which is 3,570. New weight 1,925 pounds, new moment 161,650, and new CG is 161,650 divided by 1,925, which is 83.97 inches. That is 0.77 inches further aft, and at 1,925 pounds the forward limit is still 83.0 inches, so the loading now has nearly an inch of margin instead of two tenths.

q: At 2,000 pounds with the CG at 84.0 inches, how much ballast in the baggage compartment moves the CG aft half an inch?
a: Set the new CG to 84.5 and solve. Two thousand times 84.0 plus w times 142.8, all over 2,000 plus w, equals 84.5. That gives 168,000 plus 142.8w equals 169,000 plus 84.5w, so 58.3w equals 1,000 and w is about 17 pounds. Seventeen pounds in the baggage compartment buys half an inch, which tells you how little ballast it takes and how much a forgotten bag back there matters.

q: Give me the weight shift formula and use it.
a: Weight shifted divided by total weight equals change in CG divided by distance shifted. Move a 25-pound bag from the rear seat at 118.1 to the baggage compartment at 142.8 in a 2,100-pound airplane: 25 times 24.7 equals 617.5, divided by 2,100 is 0.29 inches aft. Nothing changes except the CG, because you did not add or remove any weight, which is why a shift is the cleanest fix.
dup: How do you compute a weight shift?

q: How much does moving a passenger from the front to the back seat change things?
a: A lot. A 170-pound passenger moving from the front seats at 80.5 inches to the rear seats at 118.1 inches shifts 37.6 inches. In a 2,200-pound airplane that is 170 times 37.6 divided by 2,200, which is 2.9 inches aft. That is the biggest single lever on the airplane, so if the CG is forward, seat the heavier people in the back before you reach for ballast, and then check the aft limit.

q: What has to be checked after you add weight aft to fix a forward CG?
a: Three things. That the new gross weight is still within 2,325 pounds for this serial number; that the baggage does not exceed the 200-pound placarded limit and is secured; and that you have not now gone past the aft limit of 93.0 inches, in either the takeoff or the landing condition. Also confirm that you are still in the category you intend, since utility category on this airplane allows no baggage and no aft passengers.

q: Does fuel burn help you with a forward CG problem on this airplane?
a: No, it makes it worse. The fuel arm is 95.0 inches, which is aft of the aft CG limit of 93.0 and aft of any realistic loaded CG, so burning fuel moves the center of gravity forward. That means the landing condition, not the takeoff condition, is the critical one when you are tight against the forward limit, and you must run the numbers for both.

q: What does a forward CG actually do to the airplane?
a: It increases longitudinal stability and makes the airplane feel heavy in pitch. The tail carries a larger download, so the wing must produce more lift, which raises the stall speed and increases cruise drag, costing you speed and range. The nose is harder to raise in the flare and on a soft field takeoff, and at the extreme you may not be able to round out at all. The upside is docile stall behavior and easier recovery.

q: Could you simply put ballast in the back seat instead of the baggage compartment?
a: You could, and it is legal if it is properly secured and within the seat's structural limit, but it is less effective: the rear seat arm is 118.1 against the baggage compartment's 142.8. You need roughly twice as much weight in the back seat to achieve the same CG shift once you account for the distance from the CG. Secure it either way, because unsecured ballast becomes a projectile and a moving CG.

q: What is the difference between a TO and a FROM indication?
a: It tells you which half of the VOR's 360 radials the airplane is in, relative to the course set in the OBS. FROM means the selected course points away from the station and you are on the radial numbered the same as the course you have set; TO means the selected course points at the station and you are on the reciprocal radial. The ambiguity meter does not know your heading, only your position.

q: Which indication do you use to fix your position, and why?
a: FROM. A radial is a magnetic course outward from the station, so the FROM radial is the line you draw on the chart. Center the needle with a FROM flag, read the number under the index, find that radial on the VOR's compass rose and rule the line outward; you are somewhere on it. If you center the needle with a TO flag, the radial you are on is the reciprocal, and plotting the TO number puts you on the wrong side of the station.

q: Give me the full procedure for finding your position with one VOR.
a: Tune the frequency, identify the Morse code before you use it, rotate the OBS until the needle centers with a FROM indication, and read the radial. Draw that radial out from the station on the chart. You now have a line of position. Convert it to a point with a second radial from another VOR, with DME distance, or by seeing where the line crosses a ground feature you can identify beneath you.

q: How do you fix a position from two VORs?
a: Take a FROM radial from each and plot both; where they intersect is your position. Do them quickly and in succession so the airplane has not moved much between them. The accuracy depends on the crossing angle: near 90 degrees is excellent, and below about 30 degrees the fix is unreliable because a small bearing error smears the intersection a long way along both lines.

q: You are told you are over I-95 and asked where you are. How do you answer with one VOR?
a: Use the VOR for a line of position and the highway for the other. Center the needle FROM, read the radial, and plot it outward from the station; where that radial crosses the highway on the chart is your position. One radial plus one identifiable line feature gives a fix just as surely as two radials, and the crossing angle rule applies the same way: a radial that lies nearly along the highway gives a poor answer.

q: What are the accuracy limits of a VOR fix?
a: Line of sight, so reception depends on altitude and terrain, and the signal is unusable in the cone of confusion overhead. Bearing accuracy is limited by the permitted check tolerances: plus or minus 4 degrees on a ground checkpoint and 6 degrees in the air. Angular error becomes distance error with range, roughly one nautical mile per degree at 60 nautical miles, so a fix far from the station is a broad one.

q: How does DME turn one VOR into a fix?
a: The radial gives you a line and the DME gives you a distance arc from the station, and the two cross at one point. It is the quickest single-station fix there is. Remember that DME measures slant range, the straight line distance from the airplane to the station, not the distance over the ground, and the error is largest when you are high and close: directly overhead at 6,000 feet the readout is about one mile when the ground distance is zero.

q: Before you plot a radial, what must you confirm?
a: That the station is the one you think it is and is usable. Identify the Morse code or the recorded voice identifier, because an unmonitored or off-the-air VOR can still produce a stable, convincing and wrong needle; check for a NOTAM on the facility; confirm you are inside its service volume for your altitude; and confirm the receiver's last check is within 30 days if you intend to use it for IFR.

q: You are not sure where you are. Give me the lost procedure.
a: Climb, communicate, confess, comply, conserve. Climb for radio and radar coverage and a wider horizon, hold a heading and note the time, then try to resolve it by pilotage against a big feature such as a highway, coastline or river. Get a VOR or GPS fix. If that fails, call ATC or 121.5 and ask for help; they can give you a position, a vector and a field. Watch fuel, and land while you still have options.
dup: What is the standard procedure if you become lost on a cross country?

q: Why is a line feature the right thing to look for when you are uncertain of position?
a: Because you cannot miss it and it converts a vague area into a line. A highway, a coast, a river, a railroad or a ridge runs for miles across your track, so flying a heading that must cross it eventually turns 'somewhere around here' into 'somewhere on this line'. Pair it with one VOR radial, a DME arc or a recognizable town along the feature and you have a point.

q: What is the deliberate offset technique, and when would you use it?
a: Aim deliberately to one side of a destination or a checkpoint that sits on a line feature, so that when you reach the feature you know which way to turn instead of guessing. Ten degrees of intentional error is better than zero degrees of uncertain error. It is an old pilotage technique and it is exactly the right tool when the checkpoint is a small airport on a long road or river.

q: You have fixed your position over the highway. What now?
a: Mark it on the chart with the time. Measure the new course and distance to the next checkpoint or to the destination, work the heading for the wind you now know you have, recompute the estimate and the fuel, and only then turn onto the new heading and start the clock. Tell ATC if you are talking to anyone. Resuming the flight plan properly is what the examiner is grading, not the fix itself.

q: What does the regulation actually require you to brief your passengers on?
a: Less than you think. 14 CFR 91.107, Use of safety belts, shoulder harnesses, and child restraint systems, requires the pilot in command to ensure each person aboard has been briefed on how to fasten and unfasten that person's safety belt and shoulder harness, and to notify them to fasten them before taxi, before takeoff and before landing. For a light Part 91 airplane that is the whole legal requirement.

q: If the rule only requires belts, why give a full briefing?
a: Because the rule is a floor and the passengers are your responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3. A passenger who does not know how to open the door, where the fire extinguisher is or that he should speak up about traffic is a liability in the one minute when it matters. A paying passenger is also judging your professionalism from the briefing, and on a checkride the examiner is the client and is grading exactly that.

q: Give me the SAFETY briefing.
a: S, seat belts, shoulder harnesses and seat adjustment, how to fasten and unfasten them. A, air vents, environmental controls and air sickness bags. F, fire extinguisher, where it is and how to use it. E, exits and emergency equipment, including the ELT and survival kit. T, traffic, talking and the sterile cockpit. Y, your questions. It is the standard content; 91.107 only compels the S.

q: What does the E of SAFETY cover in a Warrior specifically?
a: That there is one cabin door, on the right side, how the handle and the latch work, and that a passenger in the right seat may be the one who has to open it; where the emergency locator transmitter is and that it works automatically; where any survival gear and first aid kit are stowed; and that if we land off airport the plan is to get out, get clear of the airplane and stay together near it.

q: What else belongs in the briefing that SAFETY does not spell out?
a: The plan for the flight and what the passenger should expect: route, time, altitude, what the airplane will sound and feel like, and anything unusual such as stalls or steep turns. Smoking, loose articles, electronic devices, and not touching the controls. What to do if I become incapacitated: hold the wings level, press the push-to-talk and say mayday on the frequency. And that the passenger may always say he is uncomfortable.

q: How does the briefing change when the passenger is paying you?
a: It becomes part of the service rather than a ritual. Brief before boarding, calmly and without jargon; explain what you will be doing and why; set expectations about weather, timing and your authority to divert or cancel; and make clear the decisions are yours. A customer who hears the no-go criteria before the flight is far easier to turn around mid-trip. Then repeat the operational items, belts and exits, at the airplane.

q: The examiner says to treat him as your client. What do you brief before takeoff?
a: Everything you would brief a paying passenger, out loud and in order: belts and harnesses, door and exits, fire extinguisher location, vents and sick bags, ELT, what the flight will involve, sterile cockpit periods and when I want quiet, and an invitation to speak up immediately about any hazard he sees, such as birds or traffic. Then the departure briefing: runway, expected performance, and what I will do if the engine quits.

q: Give me your departure briefing.
a: Runway in use and expected takeoff distance against the runway available; the airspeeds I will use and the initial heading and altitude; the departure route and first frequency. Then the abort and emergency plan: what will make me abort on the ground, and if the engine fails after takeoff with runway remaining I land straight ahead, and above a safe altitude I turn only to a chosen field. Passengers are briefed to stay quiet until I say otherwise.

q: When do you give the passenger briefing in an emergency descent to a forced landing?
a: After the memory items and once the airplane is established, not before. The order is fly the airplane, best glide and a field, memory items for the engine, then brief the passengers while you are set up and before you are busy again on short final, then back to the checklist to confirm nothing was missed. Tell them to tighten belts, show them the door latch, have them unlatch it before touchdown, and say where to meet.

q: What do you tell a passenger about the controls and the sterile cockpit?
a: That the yoke and pedals on their side move with mine and they should keep hands and feet clear unless I ask, and that bags and feet stay away from the control column and flap handle. For quiet: no conversation from taxi through 1,000 feet after takeoff, and from the descent through the landing and taxi clear, except to tell me about a hazard, which I always want to hear immediately.

q: What is the sterile cockpit rule?
a: The requirement that no flight crewmember perform any duty during a critical phase of flight other than those required for the safe operation of the aircraft, and no non-essential conversation take place. The rules are 14 CFR 121.542, Flight crewmember duties, and 14 CFR 135.100, Flight crewmember duties. Both define critical phases of flight as all ground operations involving taxi, takeoff and landing, and all other operations below 10,000 feet except cruise flight.

q: Does the sterile cockpit rule bind you on a Part 91 flight?
a: No. 121.542 and 135.100 apply to air carriers and commercial operators under Parts 121 and 135; there is no equivalent sterile cockpit regulation in Part 91. You should say that plainly rather than pretend it is binding. Then say that you brief and fly it anyway, because the accident record behind the rule is a single-pilot problem even more than an airline one.

q: Why brief it anyway if it does not apply to you?
a: Because a single pilot has no one to catch the item he drops while answering a question. The workload peaks that the rule was written around are exactly the phases where a light single kills people: taxi, takeoff and initial climb, the pattern, the approach and the landing roll. Briefing it turns a passenger from a distraction into another set of eyes, and tells him when his input is welcome and when it is not.

q: When are your high-workload periods on a typical flight?
a: Taxi, including every runway crossing; the takeoff and initial climb to about 1,000 feet AGL; the departure and frequency changes; arrival into the terminal area and the descent checklist; the traffic pattern, the approach and the landing; and the roll-out and taxi clear. Add any abnormal, which makes whatever phase you are in a critical one. The debrief item from the last candidate's ride was taxi, and that is not an accident.

q: Your passenger starts chatting on short final. What do you do?
a: Say 'standby' once, firmly and without heat, and keep flying the airplane. Do not negotiate and do not look at him. If it continues and it is degrading the approach, go around and sort it out with altitude under you. Then debrief it after landing. Having briefed the sterile period before takeoff is what makes the single word work; if you never briefed it, the fault is yours.

q: What is the one thing a passenger should always interrupt you for?
a: A hazard. Traffic, birds, smoke, a warning light, an open door, or anything that looks wrong outside. Brief it that way: 'if you see something that worries you, say it immediately, even if I am busy'. The risk of an unnecessary call is trivial; the risk of a passenger who saw the other airplane and waited for a quiet moment is not.

q: You change a frequency while crossing a runway and drift off the centerline. What went wrong?
a: In substance, yes. Changing a frequency while crossing a runway is doing two things at once in a critical phase, and the airplane drifted while the pilot was heads-down. The fix is sequencing: stop the airplane, or finish crossing and stop clear, before you touch a radio. Taxi is a critical phase in both 121.542 and 135.100 for exactly this reason, and runway incursions are overwhelmingly a distraction problem.

q: Why would you ever fly a no-flap landing?
a: Because the flaps failed, because the system is jammed or asymmetric, or because you chose to. The handbook itself says that in high wind conditions, particularly strong crosswinds, it may be desirable to approach at higher than normal speeds with partial or no flaps. Other reasons: a known electrical or mechanical problem, an airplane you do not want to slow down in turbulence, and practice so that the first one is not for real.

q: How does the approach differ without flaps?
a: It is flatter and faster. Without flaps the airplane's lift to drag ratio is better, so for the same power the descent path is shallower; you must start down earlier and plan a longer, lower final rather than trying to force the normal picture. Power controls the path and attitude controls the speed exactly as before, but you will carry less power, and you need a longer runway and no obstacle on the approach end.

q: How does the sight picture change on a no-flap landing?
a: The nose sits higher for the same airspeed because the wing needs a higher angle of attack without the flaps, so you see less of the runway over the cowl and the aiming point appears to be further down the glareshield. The approach angle itself is shallower, so the runway looks flatter and further away. Expect both, trust the airspeed and the aiming point, and do not chase the unfamiliar picture with pitch.

q: What speed do you fly on a no-flap approach?
a: A little faster than the full-flap figure, because the clean stall speed is higher than the full-flap stall speed. The handbook publishes 63 knots as the final approach speed with 40 degrees of flap, so without flaps I fly several knots above that, and I add half the gust factor if it is gusty. What I do not do is drag it in slowly; the flaps-up margin above the stall is what I am protecting.

q: Describe the roundout and touchdown without flaps.
a: Begin the roundout a little higher and more gradually, because the shallower approach path means less attitude change is needed between the approach and the landing attitude. Then expect to hold it off for a long time: the airplane is faster and cleaner, so it floats. Keep the aiming point and the centerline, let the speed bleed, and touch down on the main wheels with the nose high but short of the full-flap attitude.

q: How much more runway does a no-flap landing need?
a: Materially more, and the handbook does not publish a figure for it. The float is longer because of the extra speed and the better lift to drag ratio, and the touchdown is faster, so the ground roll is longer too. A planning rule of adding at least half again to the book landing distance is reasonable and conservative. Pick a long runway, land on the numbers you can actually make, and go around early if it is not working.

q: What are the common errors on a no-flap landing?
a: Flying the normal flap sight picture and ending up high and fast; chopping the power to make the normal descent angle and arriving low and slow; forcing the airplane onto the runway during the long float, which causes a bounce or a wheelbarrow on the nosewheel; floating past the planned touchdown point and landing long; and failing to brief the passengers or tell the tower that the landing will be a long one.

q: The flaps will not extend. How do you handle it?
a: Fly the airplane first, then diagnose. The flaps here are mechanical, operated by a cable from a handle between the front seats, not electric, so a failure means a jammed handle, a broken or stretched cable or a flap obstruction, and there is no circuit breaker to reset and no motor to fail. Do not force the handle. Plan a no-flap approach to a long runway, brief it, and tell ATC so you get the length you need.

q: What if only one flap extends?
a: Treat it as an asymmetric flap condition and do not touch the handle again. The airplane will roll toward the retracted side and you will need aileron to hold wings level; retract both only if the handle will do it cleanly, otherwise leave the configuration alone and fly it as it is. Approach faster than normal, use a long runway, keep the bank shallow, and expect the roll tendency to change as the speed decays in the flare.

q: Does raising the flaps after landing matter in this airplane?
a: Yes, for braking. The handbook says braking is most effective when the flaps are raised and back pressure is applied to the control wheel, because raising the flaps dumps lift onto the wheels. Do it after the airplane is firmly on the ground and only with your eyes outside; this airplane's flap handle is between the seats and cannot be confused with a gear lever, but the habit of waiting until clear is still the safe one.

q: Name the three stages of a stall.
a: Approaching the stall, the full stall, and the recovery. The first is the approaching or imminent stall, where the angle of attack is nearing critical and the airplane gives you the warning signs; the second is the full stall, where the critical angle of attack has been exceeded; the third is the recovery back to unstalled, controlled flight. Describe what happens in each rather than fighting over the vocabulary.

q: Describe the first stage, the approaching stall.
a: The angle of attack is approaching critical but has not reached it. You get the cues: the stall warning horn, which on this airplane sounds five to ten knots above the stall, aerodynamic buffet as separated air from the wing root strikes the tail, mushy and ineffective controls, a high nose attitude for the airspeed, and a decaying airspeed with a high sink rate. The wing is still flying and recovery costs almost no altitude.

q: Describe the full stall.
a: The critical angle of attack has been exceeded, airflow over the upper surface has separated, and the wing is producing less lift than it was a moment ago even though the angle of attack has increased. The airplane pitches down as the center of pressure moves aft and the tail download is lost, the sink rate increases sharply, and any yaw at that moment drops a wing and starts a spin. Controls are sloppy and the ailerons are untrustworthy.

q: Describe the recovery stage.
a: The stage where the angle of attack is reduced below critical and the wing starts flying again. Reduce the angle of attack first, by releasing back pressure or pushing, because nothing else recovers a stall. Then level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder, add power smoothly as needed, and return to the desired flight path with the minimum loss of altitude, retracting flaps and gear on schedule rather than all at once.

q: Someone answers 'incipient' for the first stage. Is that wrong?
a: It is the wrong word in the wrong place rather than a wrong idea. Incipient is the word the FAA uses for the second phase of a spin, between the stall break and a fully developed spin, not for the approach to a stall; the stall itself is normally described as approaching or imminent, then full, then recovery. The examiner is checking that you understand the progression, so describe what the airplane is doing at each point.

q: What is a secondary stall, and where does it fit?
a: A second stall caused by the recovery itself: the pilot raises the nose again before the wing has regained flying speed, exceeds the critical angle of attack a second time, and stalls. It is not one of the stages; it is a recovery error, and it is the commonest one on a checkride. The fix is patience, letting the airspeed build before you raise the nose, and avoiding an abrupt pull in the pitch-up after adding power.

q: Why does coordination matter so much at the stall?
a: Because a stall with yaw is a spin entry. If the ball is out at the break, the outside wing is moving faster and the inside wing is at a higher angle of attack and more deeply stalled, so it drops and autorotation begins. A skid is worse than a slip, and the instinctive correction, picking the dropping wing up with aileron, deepens the stall on that wing. Keep the ball centered with rudder through the whole maneuver.

q: Describe a stall from entry through recovery, as you would fly it for the examiner.
a: Clearing turns, then configure and set power, raise the nose to the stall attitude and hold it, keeping the ball centered with rudder and the wings level with aileron. Call the cues aloud as the horn, the buffet and the mushy controls arrive, and then the break itself. Recover by reducing angle of attack, leveling the wings, adding full power, retracting flaps on schedule, and returning to altitude and heading without a secondary stall.

q: You have an engine fire in flight. Give me the memory items for this airplane.
a: Fuel selector OFF; throttle closed; mixture to idle cut-off; electric fuel pump checked OFF; heater OFF; defroster OFF; then proceed with the power-off landing procedure. The whole idea is to stop fuel reaching the fire. Note that the electric fuel pump goes off here, which is the opposite of every other fuel emergency, and the heater and defroster go off because their air comes from a shroud on the muffler.

q: Why do the heater and defroster go off in the engine fire checklist?
a: Because on this airplane the cabin heat and the defroster are fed from a shroud around the exhaust muffler, inside the engine compartment and right next to the fire. Leaving them open is an invitation for smoke and fire gases to come into the cabin. The same shroud is why a cracked muffler is a carbon monoxide hazard, and why the first action for suspected carbon monoxide is heat off and vents open.

q: Why would you descend at VNE with an engine fire?
a: Because time is the enemy. An in-flight fire can destroy the airframe in minutes, so you get the airplane down as fast as the structure allows: descend at up to but not exceeding VNE, which is 160 KIAS on this airplane, and the high airflow may also help starve or blow out the fire and keep the flames off the fuselage. Fly it in smooth air and with care, because at VNE there is no margin for a gust.

q: Is a slip useful in an engine fire?
a: It can be. A sideslip away from the side the flames are coming from can keep fire and smoke off the cabin and away from the fuel tank in that wing while you descend. It costs you some descent efficiency and it complicates the pattern to the field, so it is a tool rather than a step: use it if the flames are coming at the cabin, and prioritize getting the airplane on the ground either way.

q: How do you declare an emergency, and what do you say?
