a: Say mayday three times on the frequency in use, or 121.5 if you have nobody, then who you are, where you are, what is wrong, what you intend to do, souls on board and fuel remaining. Squawk 7700. 14 CFR 91.3, Responsibility and authority of the pilot in command, lets you deviate from any rule to the extent required to meet the emergency, and may require a written report afterwards on request.

q: Why do controllers want souls on board and fuel remaining?
a: Souls on board tells the rescue services how many people to look for and is a number nobody can reconstruct afterwards; fuel remaining, stated in time rather than gallons, tells the controller how long you can stay airborne and how much fire risk there is at the scene. Give both unprompted when you declare, because once the workload rises you may not get the chance.

q: What do you do about the ELT in an emergency landing?
a: Nothing in the air, and then check it on the ground. A modern 406 MHz ELT fires automatically on impact through its g-switch and transmits your registration and position to the satellite system. If you have a cockpit remote switch you can turn it on manually before touchdown or after; after a landing, confirm it is transmitting by listening on 121.5, and leave it on. If it was not a real emergency, turn it off and tell Flight Service.

q: After an in-flight fire you land safely with the airplane scorched. Any reporting obligation?
a: Yes. An in-flight fire is on the immediate notification list in 49 CFR 830.5 regardless of damage or injuries, so the operator must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately by the most expeditious means available. Whether a written report follows depends: if the fire caused substantial damage it is an accident and the 10-day Form 6120.1 is due; if not, you file only if the Board asks.

q: Walk me through the types of fog, one at a time.
a: Radiation fog, from ground cooling on a clear calm night; advection fog, from warm moist air moving over a colder surface; upslope fog, from moist stable air being lifted and cooled along rising terrain; steam fog, from cold air over much warmer water; precipitation-induced or frontal fog, from warm rain falling through cool air and saturating it; and ice fog in extreme cold. All of them are the same thing in the end: a cloud sitting on the ground.

q: What is the difference between mist and fog?
a: Visibility. Both are suspended water droplets at the surface; the reporting threshold is the line between them. It is coded FG for fog when the visibility is less than 5/8 statute mile, and BR for mist when the visibility is 5/8 mile through 6 miles. Haze, HZ, is dry particles rather than water. So a METAR reading 1/2SM FG and one reading 3SM BR describe the same physical process at different intensities.

q: What cloud type is a layer of low-lying fog?
a: Stratus. Fog is simply a stratus cloud whose base is at the surface, formed by the same cooling-to-saturation process, which is why radiation fog often lifts into a low stratus deck as the morning sun warms the ground rather than burning off cleanly. If the morning TAF shows fog clearing to a 300-foot overcast, that is what has happened, and the field is still well below VFR.

q: Which fog is the one that ruins a morning departure, and when does it clear?
a: Radiation fog. It needs clear skies, light wind and high relative humidity over a land surface overnight, so it forms in the small hours in valleys and low ground and is at its worst around sunrise, exactly when you planned to leave. It burns off with a few hours of sun or lifts as the wind picks up past a few knots, but it can also simply lift into stratus and stay.

q: Why is advection fog worse news than radiation fog?
a: Because it is brought to you and it does not need night or calm. Warm moist air moving over a cooler surface, classically maritime air over cold coastal land, cools from below and saturates, and wind up to about 15 knots makes it thicker and deeper rather than dispersing it. It can form in daylight, move inland for miles, and persist for days, so a sunrise is no help and the forecast, not the clock, is what you plan on.

q: What is precipitation-induced fog and where do you meet it?
a: Warm rain falls through a layer of cooler air beneath it, evaporates into that air and saturates it, so fog forms in the rain. You meet it ahead of a warm front or around a slow-moving stationary front, often over a wide area and with a low ceiling above it. It is dangerous because it comes with precipitation and sometimes with icing, and because it forms where the pilot is already working.

q: What is steam fog and what else comes with it?
a: Cold, dry air moving over much warmer water: the water evaporates into the cold air, saturates it immediately, and the fog appears to rise off the surface like steam. It is common over lakes and rivers in autumn and early winter. It comes with low-level convective turbulence and the risk of icing in the rising, saturated air, so it is more than a visibility problem.

q: What conditions does upslope fog need, and why does it not just blow away?
a: Moist, stable air and a wind blowing it up a gradual slope. The air cools adiabatically as it rises and saturates. Unlike radiation fog it requires wind to exist and is maintained by it, so it does not burn off in the morning and can last for days as long as the flow continues, which is why it plagues the high plains east of the Rockies. It clears when the wind shifts or the air dries.

q: Hypoxia and hyperventilation feel the same. How do you tell them apart in the moment?
a: By the context, not the symptom. Ask: how high am I, and what just happened? Hypoxia goes with altitude, so above about 10,000 feet or on supplemental oxygen that may have failed, suspect it first; hyperventilation goes with stress, anxiety or a sudden fright and with visibly rapid breathing, at any altitude. Hypoxia can bring cyanosis and euphoria; hyperventilation brings tingling in the hands and around the mouth, and muscle spasm.

q: You cannot tell whether it is hypoxia or hyperventilation. What do you actually do?
a: Treat it as hypoxia first, because hypoxia is the one that kills you quickly. Put on oxygen at 100 percent flow and descend; if there is no oxygen, descend immediately. If the symptoms do not improve with oxygen, or you are at a low altitude where hypoxia is implausible, switch to the hyperventilation treatment: consciously slow the breathing rate, talk aloud, and breathe into a bag or cupped hands to restore carbon dioxide.

q: What is physically happening in hyperventilation?
a: You are breathing faster or deeper than the body needs, and blowing off carbon dioxide faster than you produce it, which raises blood pH. Oxygen is not the problem; the chemistry is. The result is dizziness, tingling in the fingers, toes and around the mouth, visual disturbance, cool clammy skin, muscle spasm, and eventually unconsciousness, at which point normal breathing resumes on its own.

q: Your passenger is panicking and breathing fast at 6,000 feet. Walk me through it.
a: Fly the airplane, then take charge of him. Get him to slow his breathing and talk to you, counting out loud or reading the checklist aloud, which forces a slower rate better than any instruction to relax; have him breathe into a paper bag or cupped hands if that is not enough. At 6,000 feet with no oxygen equipment in use, hypoxia is unlikely, but descend anyway and land if he does not settle.

q: Why does stress sit at the root of hyperventilation?
a: Because the trigger is almost always emotional rather than physical: fear, anxiety, or the sudden onset of an abnormal situation. That is also why it bites pilots at the worst time, during an emergency, when they are already loaded. The pilot who hyperventilates during an emergency makes the emergency worse by becoming a second problem, which is one more reason to brief, rehearse and slow yourself down deliberately when things go wrong.

q: What are external pressures, and why are they the dangerous element of PAVE?
a: They are the influences outside the flight that push you to go: a customer waiting, a schedule, a paid job, a passenger's event, your own desire to finish the trip. They are dangerous because they do not change anything about the airplane or the weather, only about your willingness to accept them, and they operate on you below the level of conscious decision. Every other PAVE element is a fact; this one is a motive.

q: Your cross country forecast is likely IFR and you are VFR only. What are your options?
a: Three, and I would name all three to the customer up front. Go IFR if I am rated, current and the airplane is equipped. Go part way, to the last field that is comfortably VFR, and arrange a car or an airline for the rest. Or do not go, and reschedule. Having the alternatives ready before the weather turns is what stops the pressure from producing a bad decision at the hold short line.

q: Name an accident that shows external pressure at work.
a: The Kobe Bryant helicopter accident in January 2020 is the obvious one: a charter flight continuing into deteriorating visibility toward a destination that a high-profile client expected to reach, ending in spatial disorientation and a loss of control in instrument conditions. The pattern is older than that accident and it is the same every time: a pilot who would have turned back on a personal flight pressing on because someone was waiting.

q: How do you mitigate external pressure before it reaches you?
a: Decide and publish the rules while you are calm. Set personal minimums in writing and tell the customer about them before you accept the job; build the alternatives into the plan so turning back is a plan rather than a failure; refuse to quote an arrival time you cannot guarantee; carry fuel; and agree in advance who pays for a night on the road. Then the hard conversation has already happened.

q: How is get-there-itis different from external pressure?
a: Get-there-itis, or plan continuation bias, is the internal version: the pilot's own fixation on completing the original plan even as the evidence changes. External pressure is the push from outside. They reinforce each other, and the combination is what carries a VFR pilot into instrument conditions. The defense is the same for both: pre-set go/no-go gates tied to observable facts, checked out loud at fixed points in the flight.

q: What is an accelerated stall?
a: A stall that occurs at a load factor greater than one, and therefore at a higher airspeed than the published one-g stall speed. Stall speed increases with the square root of the load factor, so at 45 degrees of bank, 1.41 g, the stall speed rises about 19 percent, and at 60 degrees, 2 g, about 41 percent. The wing has not changed its mind about the critical angle of attack; only the speed at which you reach it has changed.

q: How does an accelerated stall feel different from a normal one?
a: It is faster and sharper. The break comes with little warning at a speed that feels perfectly safe, the buffet is more pronounced and the roll-off tendency is stronger, and the airplane can be banked, turning, and at a low pitch attitude when it happens. That is why it is the stall behind the base-to-final accident: nose low, speed apparently adequate, and a tightening skidding turn.

q: How is the accelerated stall flown on the commercial checkride?
a: Clearing turns, then set up at or below maneuvering speed in the configuration the examiner specifies, roll into a coordinated turn of about 45 degrees of bank and increase back pressure smoothly and firmly until the stall warning or buffet, keeping the ball centered. Recover at the first indication by reducing angle of attack, level the wings and add power. Pick the entry altitude so that recovery is complete no lower than 3,000 feet AGL.

q: Why does the ACS set a higher recovery altitude for the accelerated stall?
a: Because the break is abrupt and the airplane can roll substantially before you catch it, so you need more room than for a straight-ahead power-off stall. Plan for recovery to be complete no lower than 3,000 feet AGL, against 1,500 feet for the other stalls. It is also the reason you keep the entry speed at or below maneuvering speed: an abrupt pull above Va can overstress the airframe before it stalls.

q: What is maneuvering during slow flight meant to demonstrate?
a: Control of the airplane at an airspeed where any further increase in angle of attack, increase in load factor or reduction in power would produce a stall warning, while flying it accurately. It shows that you can feel the airplane in the region of reversed command, that you lead with rudder, that you use power for altitude and pitch for speed, and that you are not startled by sloppy controls and a high nose.

q: Fly me slow flight with a turn and a climb, then the other way with a descent. What are you watching?
a: Airspeed first, because everything else follows it. Right rudder increases with power and decreases as the bank reverses, and the stall speed rises with bank angle, so I keep the bank shallow, lead the roll-in with rudder and keep the ball centered. In the climb I watch that the nose does not come up as power goes in, and in the descent that I do not let the speed increase out of the slow flight regime.

q: What tolerances does the commercial standard hold you to in slow flight?
a: Tighter than private: altitude within 50 feet, heading within 10 degrees, bank within 5 degrees, and airspeed plus 5 and minus 0 knots. The minus zero is the one that bites, since it means you may be fast but never slow, so set the speed a touch above the target rather than hunting for it from below. Clearing turns before entry and a positive recovery are part of the task, not optional extras.

q: What exactly is a MOA, and may you fly through one?
a: A military operations area is airspace of defined vertical and lateral limits established outside Class A to separate certain nonhazardous military training activities from IFR traffic. VFR aircraft may fly through one without a clearance or permission at any time, active or not, but should exercise extreme caution and should check with the controlling agency. IFR traffic is cleared through only if ATC can provide separation; otherwise you get rerouted.

q: How is a restricted area different, and how do you get through one?
a: A restricted area contains unusual and often invisible hazards to aircraft, such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery or guided missiles, and penetration without authorization is prohibited when the area is active. You get in by permission from the using agency, or from the controlling agency when the area has been released. Both MOAs and restricted areas are charted with their times, altitudes and controlling agency in the chart panel.

q: What is a prohibited area?
a: Airspace of defined dimensions within which the flight of aircraft is prohibited entirely, for reasons of national security or welfare. It is designated under 14 CFR Part 73, Special Use Airspace, charted with a blue hatched boundary and a P number, and unlike a restricted area it has no active and inactive times to check. There is no clearance that gets a civilian light airplane through one on a cross country.

q: The examiner points at a prohibited area on the chart and asks what it is. What do you say?
a: That it is a prohibited area, identified by its P number, that flight within it is prohibited under 14 CFR Part 73, and that I would read the special use airspace panel on the chart for the altitudes, times and controlling agency and check NOTAMs rather than rely on memory for what that particular one protects. If I do not know what is under it, I say so; being certain about the rule matters more than naming the site.

q: What is a national security area, and is it the same as a prohibited area?
a: No. A national security area is airspace of defined vertical and lateral dimensions at a location where there is a requirement for increased security of ground facilities, and pilots are requested to voluntarily avoid flying through it. It is charted with a broken magenta line and a note. When avoidance has to be mandatory, flight is prohibited by a NOTAM issued under 14 CFR 99.7, Special security instructions.

q: Describe a presidential TFR.
a: It is issued under 14 CFR 91.141, Flight restrictions in the proximity of the Presidential and other parties, and published by NOTAM. The usual shape is a 30 nautical mile outer ring and a 10 nautical mile inner core, from the surface up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL. The inner core is closed to almost everything; the outer ring allows operations on an active flight plan with a discrete code and continuous two-way communications.
dup: What does a Presidential TFR look like?

q: What is specifically prohibited inside the outer ring of a presidential TFR?
a: Flight training, practice instrument approaches, aerobatics, glider and parachute operations, banner towing, sightseeing, model aircraft, and anything else the NOTAM names, even though transit is allowed on a flight plan with a discrete code. Read the NOTAM text itself rather than assuming the standard template, because the dimensions and the exceptions change with the visit and sometimes mid-visit.

q: Name the Part 91 rules under which temporary flight restrictions are issued.
a: 14 CFR 91.137, Temporary flight restrictions in the vicinity of disaster/hazard areas; 91.138, for national disaster areas in Hawaii; 91.139, Emergency air traffic rules; 91.141, for the President and other parties; 91.143, Flight limitation in the proximity of space flight operations; and 91.145, Management of aircraft operations in the vicinity of aerial demonstrations and major sporting events. Security restrictions come separately under 14 CFR 99.7.

q: Sort these for me: MOA, restricted, prohibited, alert, warning, national security area.
a: MOA separates military training from IFR traffic and VFR may enter. Restricted contains invisible hazards and needs permission when active. Prohibited is closed outright. An alert area simply warns of a high volume of training and carries no entry restriction at all, with both pilots responsible for collision avoidance. A warning area is the same kind of hazard as a restricted area but begins 3 nautical miles out over international water. A national security area asks you to stay out voluntarily.

q: How are power transmission lines shown on a sectional, and what good are they?
a: As a line with small tower symbols along it, and the individual towers are shown as obstructions with their heights when they are tall enough to matter. They make excellent long-range line features because they run straight for miles and cross open country where nothing else is visible. They are a hazard too: the wires themselves are invisible from the air and are not all charted, so never plan to fly along one at low altitude.

q: How are railroads shown, and what makes them good or bad checkpoints?
a: As a line with regular cross ticks, with single and multiple track variants shown differently. They are good because they are straight, long and unmistakable, and the place where a railroad crosses a highway or a river beside a town is a first-class checkpoint. They are bad on their own in country with several parallel lines, and abandoned lines that still show on the ground can mislead you.

q: What makes a line feature more useful than a point feature in pilotage?
a: You cannot fly past it without noticing. A tower or a small town can slide by unseen a mile off your track, but a highway, railroad, river, coast or ridge that lies across your course has to be crossed, which turns an uncertain position into a line and gives you a reliable timing point. Use point features to confirm position along the line; use the line to catch the error in the first place.

q: You chose I-95 as a reference on your cross country. Defend the choice.
a: It is a major interstate running broadly parallel to my route, visible from altitude in any light, unmistakable in width and traffic, and it is drawn on the chart with its number so I can tie my position to exits, interchanges and the towns along it. It gives me a continuous handrail rather than a single checkpoint, so if I lose the plot between waypoints I can always fly to it and refix.

q: What are the hazards of navigating low along a linear feature?
a: Everyone else is doing the same thing, so traffic concentrates along roads, rivers and valleys; the wires and towers along a power line or a road are at your altitude; and 14 CFR 91.119, Minimum safe altitudes: General, still requires 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within a 2,000-foot horizontal radius over a congested area, and 500 feet above the surface elsewhere. Fly to the right of the feature, not over it, and keep the altitude legal.

q: What is the difference between being current and being proficient?
a: Currency is a legal state: you have met the recency requirements in 14 CFR 61.56, Flight review, and 61.57, Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, so the regulations permit the flight. Proficiency is whether you can actually fly it to standard today. Currency is the minimum the FAA will accept; proficiency is the minimum the airplane will accept, and nothing in the regulations measures the second one.

q: What is the bare legal minimum to fly passengers by day?
a: A pilot certificate, an appropriate medical or BasicMed, a flight review within the preceding 24 calendar months under 14 CFR 61.56, and three takeoffs and landings within the preceding 90 days in the same category, class and type if a type rating is required, under 14 CFR 61.57, Recent flight experience: Pilot in command. That is all. Three circuits in a familiar airplane 89 days ago makes you legal to fly your family anywhere.

q: How is night passenger currency different?
a: The three takeoffs and landings must be to a full stop, and flown between one hour after sunset and one hour before sunrise, within the preceding 90 days, in the same category, class and type. Full-stop is the detail candidates miss. Note the three definitions of night in play: this period for currency, sunset to sunrise for position lights, and the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight for logging.

q: How do you decide whether you are proficient, not just current?
a: By asking specific questions rather than how I feel: when did I last fly this airplane, this maneuver, this approach, in this weather, at this airport, with this load? If the honest answer to any of them is 'not recently', I either go and practice or I do not take that flight. Personal minimums written down beforehand, a recurrent training schedule, and an instructor who will tell me the truth are the tools.
dup: How do you decide whether you are proficient, as opposed to merely current?

q: Why does the currency and proficiency gap matter more once you fly for hire?
a: Because you will be asked to fly airplanes, routes, weather and schedules you did not choose, and the people paying you will assume that legal means competent. A commercial certificate raises the standard the public expects without changing the recency rules at all. The professional response is a personal currency standard tighter than the regulation, plus the willingness to say that you are legal but not proficient for a particular trip.

q: The three stages of a stall. Go.
a: Approaching the stall, the full stall, and the recovery. Approaching: angle of attack nearing critical, horn and buffet, mushy controls, high sink rate, wing still flying. Full: critical angle of attack exceeded, airflow separated, lift falling away and the nose dropping. Recovery: reduce angle of attack first, level the wings, add power, return to the flight path without a secondary stall. This is the question the last candidate missed.

q: You hit a runway light. Do you have to report it, and where does the rule live?
a: The rule is 49 CFR Part 830, an NTSB rule, not a Federal Aviation Regulation. Test it: nobody was killed or seriously injured, and damage to gear, wheels, tires, flaps or wingtips is expressly excluded from substantial damage, so on those facts it is an incident and no report is required. It becomes reportable if the airplane takes substantial damage, or if damage to the light and its cabling exceeds $25,000 under 830.5.

q: Which items in 830.5 will never apply to your Warrior?
a: The ones written for transport aircraft: in-flight failure of electrical or hydraulic systems, and sustained loss of thrust from two or more engines, which apply only to large multiengine aircraft of more than 12,500 pounds maximum certificated takeoff weight; an evacuation using an emergency egress system; ACAS resolution advisories on an IFR flight plan; helicopter rotor blade damage; and the air carrier wrong-runway and runway incursion items.

q: Is a flap position light required? Show me the whole chain of reasoning.
a: There is no MEL, so I start at 14 CFR 91.205 for day VFR and run the list: it requires a landing gear position indicator on a retractable and says nothing about flaps. Then the kinds of operation equipment list in Section 2, which does not list one; then the airplane's equipment list; then any airworthiness directive or STC supplement. Nothing requires it, so it is not required equipment, and if it were fitted and inoperative I would work 91.213(d).

q: A non-pilot customer hires you to fly his airplane, then rents one when his is grounded. Talk me through both halves.
a: First half: he supplies the airplane and keeps operational control, I supply pilot services only, so it is Part 91 and my commercial certificate covers it. Second half turns on the same question. If he rents in his own name and still decides the flight, nothing changes. If I rent the airplane and then carry him for compensation, I am supplying aircraft and crew for hire and that needs a Part 119 certificate. If it is unclear, I decline or call the FSDO.

q: What documents must the pilot have to fly? Be careful with this one.
a: Pilot certificate, an appropriate medical certificate or BasicMed documentation, and government-issued photo identification, per 14 CFR 61.3. The Restricted Radiotelephone Operator Permit is an FCC document required only for international operations and does not belong on this list. Say it that way and you have turned the standard trap into a point in your favor; volunteer the permit only when the question turns to flying outside the country.

q: Your handbook has no kinds of operation equipment list. Now what?
a: Then the airplane is one of the many certificated before the GAMA format made the list standard, and I say so rather than inventing one. Required equipment then comes from 14 CFR 91.205 and whatever other operating rule applies to the flight, the airplane's own equipment list, the type certificate data sheet, and any airworthiness directive or STC supplement. For an inoperative item, 91.213(d) is the path, with a placard and a hazard determination.

q: Simulated engine fire. Memory items and then what?
a: Fuel selector OFF, throttle closed, mixture idle cut-off, electric fuel pump checked OFF, heater OFF, defroster OFF, then the power-off landing procedure. Descend fast, up to but not exceeding VNE, 160 KIAS, because an airframe fire is measured in minutes. Declare with mayday on the frequency or 121.5, squawk 7700, give souls and fuel, brief the passengers once established, and check the ELT after landing.

q: The CG is inside the envelope but close to the forward limit. What do you do about it?
a: Move weight aft or add it aft, and show the arithmetic. The baggage compartment arm is 142.8 inches, far behind the rear seats at 118.1 and the aft limit at 93.0, so it is the strongest lever: at 2,000 pounds, 17 pounds of baggage moves the CG half an inch aft. Then recheck gross weight against 2,325 pounds, the 200-pound baggage placard, the aft limit, and the landing case, because burning fuel here moves the CG forward.

q: Time, fuel and distance to climb. How do you get the number?
a: By subtraction, not by one lookup. Enter the chart at the departure field's pressure altitude and temperature, read time, fuel and distance; enter again at cruise altitude and temperature; subtract the first set from the second. Add the start, taxi and run-up allowance, and convert the chart's still air distance into ground distance using the climb groundspeed. Higher temperature and higher altitude increase all three numbers.

q: What is the significance of the stadium symbol on the chart?
a: It marks a large stadium and flags a standing restriction: no flight below 3,000 feet AGL within 3 nautical miles of a stadium seating 30,000 or more during an MLB, NFL, NCAA Division One football or major motor speedway event, from one hour before to one hour after. It is a standing FDC NOTAM issued under 14 CFR 99.7, Special security instructions, and it is not drawn on the chart, so NOTAMs are the only way to know.

q: What are the two types of stress and how do they show up in a pilot?
a: Acute and chronic. Acute is the short-term response to a present demand, such as a warning light or a runway change, and it narrows attention and causes fixation; chronic is the continuing, unresolved load of money, a job or a family problem, and it shows up as fatigue, poor decisions and indifference to risk. Chronic stress consumes the reserve you need for the acute events of a flight, so the two stack. Both are the S in IMSAFE.

q: Give me the passenger briefing you would use with a paying client.
a: SAFETY, delivered before boarding and again at the airplane. Seat belts and harnesses, how to fasten and unfasten; air vents and sick bags; fire extinguisher location; exits, the single right-side door and its latch, plus the ELT and survival gear; traffic and talking, meaning the sterile cockpit periods and the standing invitation to call out any hazard; and your questions. Only the seat belt item is actually required, by 14 CFR 91.107.

q: You are crossing a runway and the controller gives you a frequency change. What do you do?
a: Finish crossing, get clear of the hold short line, stop the airplane, and then touch the radio. Acknowledge the instruction but do not start head-down work in a critical phase. Taxi is a critical phase of flight in both 14 CFR 121.542 and 135.100, and runway incursions are overwhelmingly a distraction problem. This is exactly the item the last candidate was debriefed on: too many things at once, a drift off the centerline, then a recovery.
